stories.headline: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, agents that fix failing pull requests and can approve routine ones under a team's written policy
stories.summary: The beta adds a 'PR Steward' that repairs CI failures and merge conflicts and 'Claude Approvals' that signs off on changes a policy file allows.

p: Anthropic launched Claude Ship on Monday, Nov 23, for Claude Team and Enterprise plans, for repositories on GitHub. It bundles three agents. Code Review, already generally available, comments on pull requests. PR Steward (beta) fixes failing CI checks, resolves merge conflicts, and addresses Code Review's feedback, and comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back. Claude Approvals (beta) approves pull requests that meet an approval policy the team writes in plain language as a file in the repository; the policy can draw on Code Review findings and the company's own classifiers.

Teams choose where it runs, the review depth (Quick, Standard, or Deep), which changes get escalated to a human, and a monthly spending limit. Anthropic recommends starting Claude Approvals in observe-only mode on a single repository. Its blog post said: 'On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.'

table: Review depth, escalation rules, observe-only mode, monthly spend cap
sections.note: From TechCrunch and SiliconANGLE coverage of Anthropic's Nov 23 announcement.

p: **Pull request (PR):** a proposed code change submitted for review before it is merged into the main codebase.
**CI (continuous integration):** automated tests and checks that run on every proposed change; a 'failing CI check' blocks a merge.
**Required approval:** many teams configure GitHub so a change can't merge until someone approves it. Claude Approvals fills that slot with an agent.

Code review has become the bottleneck as agents write more code: humans can't read it all. Claude Ship is Anthropic's bet that the fix is letting an AI approve the boring changes, under rules the team writes. The real question is the policy, not the model. A vague policy plus an agent that both fixes and approves code means one vendor's system can author and sign off on the same change, which weakens the 'two sets of eyes' that review exists for. Security and compliance teams (SOC 2, change management) will want to see whether an AI approval counts.
The observe-only default is the right starting point. Watch for whether Anthropic publishes data on how often Claude Approvals would have approved changes humans rejected.

stories.headline: OpenAI and Cisco open-source Shirudo, which lets AI agents write temporary kernel-level shields for unpatched Linux systems
stories.summary: Agents generate signed eBPF 'shields' that block a vulnerable code path on a running machine until the real patch ships; it is an early project with one worked demo.

p: OpenAI and Cisco released Shirudo (Japanese for 'shield') on Monday, Nov 23, as an open-source Linux runtime. When a vulnerability is found, an agent investigates it, reproduces the exploit, and builds a shield: a small program, mostly eBPF, that blocks the vulnerable code path on a running system without a restart. Shields are cryptographically signed and checked before loading, and a TPM keeps a verifiable record of what was loaded or removed. Teams can run a shield in monitor mode first; Cisco says it 'graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands.'

In a controlled test, the team used Codex to generate a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it to a running Elasticsearch process; it blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt and Elasticsearch kept running. Cisco says it also tested a PHP flaw. The code is on GitHub under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed BSD and GPL. The Hacker News reports it builds on Tetragon, the eBPF security tool from Cisco's Isovalent unit.
**eBPF:** a Linux feature that lets small, verified programs run inside the kernel to watch or filter what the system does, without changing kernel code or rebooting.
**Virtual patching:** blocking an exploit at runtime while the real code fix is tested and rolled out.
**TPM (Trusted Platform Module):** a security chip that can attest what software was loaded on a machine.

AI is shrinking the time between a bug's disclosure and a working exploit, while patching still takes days or weeks. Shirudo aims at that gap. The idea of runtime shielding is not new (web firewalls and intrusion-prevention tools do it), but having an agent write a precise shield per vulnerability is.

Be measured about it. OpenAI calls it 'a first step,' much of the feature list is written as what 'we are designing,' and the public evidence is one demo. An AI-written program running in the kernel can break legitimate traffic, which is why both companies are asking contributors to 'show us where it breaks.' The signing and monitor-first design is the part that makes it usable in production; check it before trusting it.
A technical webinar on Dec 15, outside testing results, and whether Linux distributions or cloud providers adopt it.

stories.headline: Nvidia's board reverses itself and reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock jumps more than 30%
stories.summary: Eleven days after Huang resigned, the board voted unanimously to bring him back, citing input from 'senior levels' of the US government, while its foreign-intelligence investigation continues.

p: Nvidia announced on Monday, Nov 23, that its board had unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and a board director, effective immediately. The company filed the press release with the SEC as an 8-K. The board said it acted after "a series of discussions and meetings" that left it satisfied with Huang's "candor and ability to lead NVIDIA," and that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that made it confident his return "poses no national security risk." The release does not say who in government gave that input.

This reverses the board's position of only six days earlier. On the Nov 17 earnings call, chairman Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, and it had hired Heidrick & Struggles to run a CEO search. Huang resigned on Nov 12 after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former head of Megaspeed, a Singapore company US authorities have investigated over suspected chip smuggling to China. President Trump had pushed publicly for his return, most recently in a Truth Social post late Sunday. According to an AIweekly account of a CNBC interview, Trump said he spoke with the board "directly and indirectly," that Huang "did nothing wrong," and that he had raised the case with Xi Jinping.

Jones stays as chair and said the board "believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA." Colette Kress, interim CEO since Nov 12, goes back to being CFO only. Huang said he takes the job back "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." The release also sets out governance changes: the independent-director committee investigating reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort "will proceed to conclusion," with his cooperation; a new National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors will oversee trade compliance; and Nvidia is searching for a new chief compliance officer who will report to the board's governance committee.

table: Nvidia market value, Nov 11 close to Nov 20 low
sections.note: Index and stock moves from The Motley Fool's midday report as of 11:31 a.m. ET; figures shifted through the session and are not closing prices. Market value range from Fox Business.

p: **8-K:** the form US public companies file with the SEC to disclose major events, such as a CEO change, within four business days.
**Independent directors:** board members with no management role or material business ties to the company, used for investigations so that the people being examined do not oversee them.

The market's verdict was immediate: much of last week's AI selloff was about Nvidia's leadership vacuum, and Huang's return erased a large part of it in one morning. That says something about how much of the AI trade still rests on one company and one founder.

The governance story is less tidy. A board that said it would not rehire Huang reversed course within a week, after the President lobbied for it in public and, by his own account, in private. The key justification, government input on national security, is unnamed and unpublished. The questions that caused the crisis are still open: the board's own investigation, the SEC's accounting inquiry, Treasury's export-compliance questions, and congressional requests for Huang to testify. Reinstatement does not answer any of them; it means Huang will lead the company while they are answered.

For people building on Nvidia hardware, nothing changes operationally today. The practical risk shifts from 'who runs Nvidia' to 'what the investigations find' and whether new compliance controls slow sales into restricted markets.

Whether Huang still appears for the House transcribed interview requested for Dec 1 and the Senate Banking hearing requested for Dec 3, the result of the board committee's investigation, Nvidia's delayed 10-Q, and how Treasury responds when its 10-day window for answers ends around Nov 25. Fox reported that the CEO search had approached Arm's Rene Haas; Arm said Monday he has extended his contract through 2033.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in stock, pitching the deal as security for AI agents
stories.summary: The all-stock deal, confirmed a day after reports of talks, combines endpoint and network security into a company with more than $10 billion in recurring revenue.

p: CrowdStrike announced on Monday, Nov 23, a definitive agreement to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal with an enterprise value of about $43.9 billion. Zscaler shareholders will get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share, about $260.41 at CrowdStrike's Nov 20 close and a roughly 34% premium to Zscaler's price that day. Existing CrowdStrike holders will own about 84.1% of the combined company and Zscaler holders about 15.9%.

Both boards approved it unanimously. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry, who with his affiliates holds about 34% of Zscaler's shares, has signed an agreement to vote for it; he will keep running the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike's board. The deal needs Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028. CrowdStrike announced the deal alongside its fiscal third-quarter results, which showed revenue up 28% to $1.58 billion and ARR of $6.26 billion.

The companies framed it around AI. CEO George Kurtz said that "safety is required to let AI in" and that he sees a path to become "the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen." Chaudhry said "AI agents are rapidly becoming the new weakest link." In midday trading Zscaler rose about 15% and CrowdStrike fell about 11%, per The Motley Fool.

sections.note: From CrowdStrike's deal and earnings releases filed with the SEC on Nov 23. Synergy figures are company targets.

p: **All-stock deal:** the buyer pays with its own shares instead of cash, so the sellers' payout rises and falls with the buyer's stock price until closing.
**ARR (annual recurring revenue):** the yearly value of subscriptions in place, the main growth metric for security software firms.
**Zero trust:** a network design that checks every user and device on every request instead of trusting anything inside the corporate network. It is Zscaler's core business.

This is the largest cybersecurity acquisition announced this year and the clearest bet yet that companies will buy AI-agent security from a big platform instead of from specialists. CrowdStrike sees what happens on laptops and servers; Zscaler sees traffic between users, apps, and the internet. An agent that holds credentials and calls tools crosses both, which is the logic behind the pitch.

The caveats: the 'AI safety' language is marketing on top of a conventional consolidation deal, the synergy figures are targets, and the CrowdStrike share drop shows investors are not sure the price is right. Closing is more than a year away and needs antitrust review, and because the payment is in stock, the deal's dollar value will move with CrowdStrike's share price until then.

CrowdStrike's S-4 filing with Zscaler's proxy statement, antitrust review, and whether rivals such as Palo Alto Networks, which agreed last week to buy Applied Compute, respond with deals of their own.

stories.headline: OpenAI publishes its pretraining loss numbers and asks labs to agree on limits they won't cross, and Microsoft shares its own
stories.summary: Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposes shared 'common limits' tied to measures like perplexity; Microsoft AI says its MAI-2 base model scores 0.819 on OpenAI's test.

p: On Nov 22, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published "Perplexity and Intelligence," disclosing how OpenAI's pretrained models have scored on an internal held-out test drawn from OpenAI's own codebase. GPT-3.5 scored a log-perplexity of about 0.99, GPT-4 about 0.91, and later models dropped below 0.8, reaching about 0.76. Lower means the model predicts the held-out text better.

Pachocki argues this number tracks capability well enough to anchor coordination. He asks developers to "jointly endeavour to establish shared norms" and "common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements," that they would commit not to cross until the ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches "a certain concrete milestone." He says OpenAI expects "further transformative capabilities" in the ~0.68 to 0.7 range, but the post does not name a specific limit or use the word pause. It lists its own caveats: labs use different test sets and data, the number does not capture gains from reasoning or other post-training, there is an unknown floor, and publishing it tells competitors where OpenAI stands.

Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman replied on X early Nov 23 that Microsoft "fully support[s]" the initiative and that MAI-2 Base scores 0.819 on OpenAI's test set (MAI-1 Base: 0.878), which he put in "the same ballpark" as OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol base model. Per CellCog's account, he called Microsoft's access to OpenAI's test set "a special case," suggested other labs report bits per byte instead, and did not endorse any limit value. No other major lab had published a number as of Monday.

sections.note: Log-perplexity on OpenAI's internal held-out evaluation set. OpenAI figures from its Nov 22 post; Microsoft figures from Suleyman's X post as reported by CellCog.

p: **Log-perplexity (cross-entropy loss):** the average penalty a model takes for not predicting the next token of test text. Lower is better. Small drops near the bottom of the curve can mean large capability gains.
**Base model:** the model straight out of pretraining, before instruction tuning or reasoning training.
**Bits per byte:** a version of the same measure normalized by raw text length, so models with different tokenizers can be compared.

This is the first time a frontier lab has published a running capability metric for its unreleased pretraining work and proposed using it as a tripwire. That is a real transparency step, and Microsoft matching it the same night shows it can work across companies that share infrastructure.

It is also a weak tripwire as designed. The number only compares cleanly on the same test set and tokenizer, which is why Microsoft could report against OpenAI's and other labs cannot without help. It ignores reasoning and agent training, which drive much of today's capability gains. And there are no commitments yet, only a request to negotiate them. Whether Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI, or the Chinese labs report anything is the real test.
Responses from other labs, whether anyone proposes a shared public test set, and whether US or EU officials pick up loss thresholds as an alternative to compute thresholds in rules.

stories.headline: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX's AI unit, saying Grok's 'spicy mode' made sexual deepfakes, including of children
stories.summary: The coordinated consumer-protection suits are the first by states over Grok's image tools and argue the company falsely told users they were protected.

p: Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed separate but coordinated lawsuits on Monday, Nov 23, against the Musk companies behind Grok. Virginia's defendants include SpaceX Super Intelligence Corp., SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC, X Corp., and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.; SpaceX Super Intelligence is the structure that now houses X, xAI, and Grok. Oregon filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court. SpaceX had told investors in an October securities filing that Virginia was weighing legal action, The Next Web reports.

The states allege the companies launched Grok's "spicy mode," which can turn a photo of a real person into a sexual or nude image or video, without adequate safeguards, and misled people about Grok's safety. Jones said: "Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false." Rayfield said the company "knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place." Virginia's suit cites its Consumer Protection Act and seeks an injunction, restitution, and penalties. The states hired the firm of former New Jersey Attorney General Matthew Platkin to run the cases.

The suits rely on a Center for Countering Digital Hate study of X between Dec 29, 2025, and Jan 8, 2026. No company response to the suits was reported; xAI has argued in a separate Minnesota case that it bans nonconsensual sexual images and sues people who get around its safeguards. The allegations have not been tested in court.

table: Sexualized images posted on X, Dec 29 to Jan 8
Child images still public a week after detection
sections.note: Center for Countering Digital Hate figures as cited in the lawsuits, per IBTimes via Yahoo News.

p: In January, 35 attorneys general sent xAI a letter of concern. This is the step after that: lawsuits under ordinary consumer-protection law, with no AI-specific statute needed. The legal theory is deception, that the company promised safety it did not deliver, which is the same route states have used against social media companies and is harder to defeat with free-speech arguments than a content rule.

For anyone shipping image or video generation, the lesson is that public safety claims are now evidence. Saying users are protected while shipping a feature built for sexual edits of real photos is what the states are targeting.
Whether other states that signed the January letter file their own suits, xAI's response, and California's investigation into Grok images, open since January.

stories.headline: Zhipu ships GLM-5.4 to its coding-plan subscribers, a reported 750-billion-parameter model that reuses layers, with no benchmarks yet
stories.summary: Z.ai says looping part of the network gives the depth of a much bigger model, but there is no API, no open weights, and no published evaluation.

p: Z.ai (Zhipu AI) made GLM-5.4 available to all GLM Coding Plan subscribers on Monday, Nov 23. Z.ai's Zixuan Li announced it on X at about 04:18 UTC. It is available in ZCode and Z.ai Chat, and in Claude Code as "glm-5.4[1m]", which selects a 1-million-token context window. Z.ai says the model adds vision and stronger coding, and some plan tiers get 50% more usage than they had with GLM-5.3.

It is Z.ai's first flagship built as a "Loop Transformer." According to DEV Community and AIweekly summaries of Z.ai's blog, it has about 750 billion parameters and runs 28 of its layers twice per forward pass, adding depth without adding weights; Z.ai claims intelligence "comparable to 2T-3T parameter models." Early on Monday TechNode reported that Z.ai had not yet published architecture, parameter, or benchmark details, so treat these figures as the company's claims.

table: Planned after safety hardening, no date
sections.note: From TechNode, CellCog, ChainCatcher, and DEV Community coverage of Z.ai's announcements on Nov 23.

p: **Loop Transformer:** a model that sends its hidden state through the same block of layers more than once, so it computes more per token without storing more weights. Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini uses the same idea.
**Coding plan:** a flat-rate subscription that gives a usage quota inside coding tools, instead of paying per token through an API.

Looping is spreading quickly from small open models to frontier-scale ones, because it buys more reasoning compute per token without a bigger memory bill. But the '2T-3T' comparison is a claim without evidence: no benchmarks, no model card, and no independent access beyond subscribers. Users also report it can get stuck in very long thinking loops.
Zhipu's earlier GLM-5 models shipped open weights, which made them a common cheap alternative for coding agents. Until 5.4's weights or API arrive, it matters mainly to people already on Z.ai's plan.
A technical report with benchmarks, API pricing, and the open-weights release and license.

stories.headline: Trump posts that Nvidia's board should rehire Jensen Huang, his most direct appeal yet, as Nvidia futures rebound
stories.summary: The board has already said it will not bring Huang back, and the Treasury Secretary said a day earlier that Washington first wants to know 'where the buck stops.'
stats: Nvidia futures early Monday, per BeInCrypto

p: Late Sunday night US time, President Trump wrote on Truth Social: "I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A." Seeking Alpha timestamped its report 11:52 PM ET Sunday; The National and Investing.com describe it as a Monday post, which matches the time in Asia and Europe.

It goes further than his earlier comments. On Nov 16 he said he "certainly would not mind seeing" Huang reinstated, and on Friday he told reporters he wanted Huang to apologize and come back. Huang resigned on Nov 12 after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former head of Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which US authorities have investigated since 2024 over suspected chip smuggling to China. Officials have stopped short of calling her a spy; Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN on Sunday that "there are chips that have ended up in places that they should not," per The National.

Nvidia's position has not changed. Chairman Harvey Jones said on the Nov 17 earnings call that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO" and has hired Heidrick & Struggles to run the CEO search. No new response from Nvidia or Huang to the post was reported by Monday morning.

sections.note: Friday close and Oct 29 comparison from BeInCrypto via Yahoo Finance; weekly drop and futures from BeInCrypto and Yahoo Finance's live blog. Premarket moves can reverse by the open; Yahoo's blog showed Nvidia up about 8.9% at one point.

p: A president cannot reinstate a CEO; only the board can. What the post does is raise the political cost of the board's stance while its own Wachtell Lipton investigation, an SEC accounting inquiry, an FBI investigation, and congressional requests are still open. It also cuts against the message from Treasury Secretary Bessent, who said on Sunday that the government first wants to know whether compliance failures "went all the way to the top."

Be careful reading the stock rebound as a verdict on the post. Futures were rising across the market after seven straight losing days for the S&P 500, and analysts quoted by Bloomberg called a bounce "always likely." Nvidia's move is bigger than the index, which suggests some traders are betting on a Huang return, but the board has given no sign of one. For people building on Nvidia hardware, nothing changes operationally; the open question is who sets Nvidia's strategy and how it handles export compliance.
Whether the board responds, the end of Bessent's roughly 10-day window for answers around Nov 25, and the requested congressional interviews with Huang on Dec 1 and Dec 3.

stories.headline: South Korea, Taiwan, and China move to prop up their stock markets after the AI selloff, and the Kospi still falls more than 3%
stories.summary: Seoul readied a fund last used in 2008, Taiwan restricted short selling, and China eased margin rules, while US futures pointed to a rebound.

p: After last week's slide in AI and chip stocks, regulators across Asia announced support measures over the weekend, CNBC reported. South Korea's finance ministry said on Sunday its securities stabilization fund, valued at 10.76 trillion won (nearly $8 billion), is ready for immediate activation; the fund was last used in 2008. Korea is also relaxing share buyback limits for three months from Nov 24 and running a "special intensive monitoring period" for illegal short selling.

Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission barred short sales below the previous day's close, with an exception for hedging by securities and futures firms, and raised the minimum short-selling margin from 130% to 150%. China's Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Beijing exchanges will cut the minimum margin for buying shares on borrowed money from 100% to 80% starting Nov 30.

The results on Monday were mixed. Korea's Kospi fell as much as 5% before closing down about 3.3% at 4,708.54, with Samsung Electronics down about 3.1% and SK Hynix down about 2.5%. Taiwan's index reversed early losses to gain more than 2%, and China's CSI 300 slipped about 0.7%. In the US, S&P 500 futures were up about 2.6% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 3% before the open.

table: 10.76 trillion won, ready but not yet deployed
sections.note: Asia figures from CNBC (via Jingletree syndication), Superpower Daily, and Lapaas Voice; Kospi close from Lapaas Voice (CNBC gave about 3.26% intraday). US figures from Yahoo Finance's live blog. One outlet reported Taiwan also activated its NT$500 billion stabilization fund; we could not confirm that elsewhere.

p: **Short selling:** borrowing shares and selling them, betting the price falls so you can buy back cheaper. Banning shorts below the last close is meant to stop sellers from piling on during a drop.

**Margin requirement:** how much of your own cash you must put up when buying with borrowed money. Cutting China's minimum from 100% to 80% lets investors borrow more, which can add buying power and also risk.
**Stabilization fund:** a pool of money, often from state-linked institutions, set aside to buy stocks in a panic and slow the fall.

These markets are heavily tied to the AI hardware boom: Samsung and SK Hynix make the memory in AI servers, and TSMC makes most leading AI chips. When governments step in this way, it is a sign they see the selloff as a risk to their wider economies, not just to a few stocks.

Interventions like these usually slow a decline rather than reverse it; the Kospi fell anyway on Monday. The real driver is still US sentiment on AI spending, Nvidia's legal problems, and a Fed that markets expect to raise rates on Dec 9. A one-day bounce in US futures does not settle any of those.
Whether Korea actually deploys its fund, how US stocks finish Monday in a holiday-shortened week, and the Fed decision on Dec 9.

stories.headline: Bessent says the administration needs to know whether Nvidia's China compliance failures 'went all the way to the top'
stories.summary: On CBS's Face the Nation, the Treasury Secretary said Washington is pressing Nvidia's interim management, lead directors, and lawyers for answers on who ran export compliance.
stats: End of his 10-day window for answers

p: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday, Nov 22, on CBS's "Face the Nation" that the US government has "been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers, and we do need answers" from Nvidia about its chip sales to China, Reuters reported.

He said the government wants to see "who was in charge of compliance there," and asked: "Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle level? Did it go all the way to the top?" He added that "it behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was," and said he expected the board to "come up with some very fulsome and robust answers."

Asked whether President Trump was right to say on Friday that he would like former CEO Jensen Huang to apologize and return, Bessent said: "I think we have to see where the buck stops." Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones has said the board will not rehire Huang, according to Reuters.

This is the clearest public statement yet that the administration's interest is not limited to Huang personally. Asking whether problems reached "the top" also implies looking at the managers and the compliance function that remain at Nvidia, which matters for a company already facing an SEC accounting inquiry, an FBI investigation, congressional requests, and a proposed class action, per Reuters.

It also sits awkwardly beside Trump's openness to Huang returning. Bessent did not endorse that idea; he deferred it until the facts are in. For people building on Nvidia hardware, nothing changes operationally today, but the tone suggests the export-compliance question will shape Nvidia's leadership choices, not just its legal bills.
Bessent's 10-day window for Nvidia's board and outside counsel to respond ends around Nov 25. Jensen Huang's requested House interview is Dec 1 and the Senate Banking hearing request is Dec 3.

stories.headline: Anthropic capped IPO deal teams at four bankers and sought six-month bans on working for rivals, Reuters reports
stories.summary: An exclusive Reuters account of 'Project Lantern' says Anthropic ran its 22-bank IPO with unusually tight controls, much as SpaceX did in June.

p: Reuters reporters Echo Wang and Milana Vinn reported on Sunday, Nov 22, that Anthropic told some of its 22 underwriters to limit their deal teams to four senior bankers. It also asked senior bank officers to sign agreements barring core deal-team members from working with rivals including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek, and Hugging Face for six months after the listing.

Instead of emailing PDFs, Anthropic shared documents through NetRoadshow, a platform that logs access, watermarks each banker's name on the page, and blocks saving copies. Reuters says it had reported details of Anthropic's draft S-1 nearly four weeks before the filing became public. The night before the planned Nov 10 launch, a law firm sent banks a PDF with the wrong price range and share information and asked them to disregard it; the corrected amended filing (S-1A) went out around 2 a.m. New York time, leaving banks several hours to sign off.

Banks still collected more than half a billion dollars in fees from the Nov 19 listing, internally called "Project Lantern," Reuters says. Like SpaceX, Anthropic negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the extra over-allotment shares. Anthropic, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley, the lead banks on both IPOs, declined to comment.

sections.note: All figures as reported by Reuters.

p: **Underwriters:** the banks that buy shares from the company and resell them to investors, earning a fee called the spread.
**Over-allotment (greenshoe) shares:** extra shares, usually up to 15% of the deal, that banks can sell to support the price. Paying zero spread on them means the banks did that work for free.
**S-1A:** an amended version of the registration statement a company files with the SEC before an IPO.

The leverage has shifted to the issuer. When a deal is "oversubscribed many times over," as Reuters says both SpaceX and Anthropic were, banks accept terms they would normally refuse because the league-table credit and fees are still worth it. University of Florida professor emeritus Jay Ritter told Reuters he doesn't think most companies will be able to demand zero spread on over-allotment shares, so expect this to stay a mega-deal exception.

The rival bans are the more unusual part. They keep a handful of bankers who saw Anthropic's internals away from competitors for a while, but they are contracts with individuals' employers, not a legal wall, and they don't stop other teams at the same banks from working for OpenAI.
Disclosure: Latent is produced with Claude, which is made by Anthropic.

stories.headline: FT traces the Megaspeed chip pipeline to Inspur's US arm and a Prince Group executive, as reported by Seoul Economic Daily
stories.summary: The Financial Times reportedly mapped how Nvidia chips moved from a California subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese firm, through Alice Huang's Megaspeed, into China.
stats: Inspur added to US Entity List

p: The Financial Times published an investigation on Saturday, Nov 21, into how Nvidia chips reached China through Southeast Asia, based on interviews and corporate registry filings. Latent could not read the FT article directly; the details here come from Seoul Economic Daily's machine-translated account of it, published Sunday, so treat specifics as reported, not confirmed.

Per that account, the FT describes three layers. First, a legal buyer: Inspur, once a major Nvidia partner, was put on the US Entity List in 2023 for alleged military support, but its California subsidiary Aivres was not and kept buying from Nvidia. An offshore shell set up to buy from Aivres later grew into Megaspeed, with Alice Huang as its "public face." Second, customers such as cloud providers that were not themselves violating controls. Third, an underground route into China: the FT links Hu Xiaowei, described as second-in-command of Cambodia's Prince Group, which US and UK authorities have accused of running online scam operations, to Century Huatong, a Chinese gaming and AI data center company, through a game partnership and an indirect stake.

The report says a Huatong subsidiary set up distribution firms and that Alice Huang and her sister controlled a joint venture with Huatong. Tencent owns 10.1% of Huatong, and Tencent and Alibaba are described as its customers; the report does not accuse either of wrongdoing. Separately, the Wall Street Journal has reported that a Singapore-based Chinese businessman, Li Ming, was central to Megaspeed's decisions and that Huang may have been a figurehead. No responses from the named parties were included in the account Latent read.

**Entity List:** a Commerce Department blacklist. US companies need a license, usually denied, to sell controlled technology to listed firms. Subsidiaries are not automatically covered, which is the gap this story turns on.
**Neocloud:** a newer cloud company that mainly rents out GPUs for AI, as opposed to the big general clouds.

If accurate, this explains how a blacklisted company's chips could keep flowing legally on paper: each link in the chain was technically allowed, and the violation happened only at the last hop into China. That is why Washington's new rules focus on subsidiaries and remote access, and why Bessent's question about who ran Nvidia compliance (see the lead story) matters: the warning signs here were corporate-structure ones a compliance team could check.

Caution is warranted. This is a secondhand, translated summary of a paywalled investigation, and the Prince Group link rests on business ties, not on evidence in this account that Hu personally moved chips.
Whether Commerce adds Aivres or Megaspeed-linked firms to the Entity List, and whether Nvidia's board addresses these supply-chain links in its response to Treasury.

stories.headline: Lean and Mathlib communities certify Alpöge's Claude-assisted Riemann proof as correct, though no human-readable proof exists yet
stories.summary: A joint statement endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative says both the statement and the 17-million-line proof check out; it does not cover the generalized version, and mathematicians still cannot read the argument.
stats: Lines of Lean in the proof

p: On Saturday, Nov 21 (posted 13:55 UTC), the Lean community blog published "Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis," a joint statement by "the Lean and Mathlib communities," endorsed by the Lean FRO (the nonprofit that develops Lean) and the Mathlib Initiative. It says: "We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct," and that they have "full confidence" in Levent Alpöge's proof. The statement names no individual signatories.

It sets out four checks. The theorem proved is Mathlib's own `RiemannHypothesis` definition, which was written and vetted before this proof existed. Dozens of people report the library compiles and reproduces the same proof export. Two tools, comparator and con-leche, confirmed the proved theorem matches that definition, which was the step still pending in Saturday afternoon's edition. And the proof was accepted by Lean's own kernel plus independent checkers, including con-leche and con-ron, which come with a formal proof that they cannot accept a false proof (relative to set theory), all run on an "inert export" so that no code hidden in the Lean files could interfere.

MIT's Andrew Sutherland, whose logs underpin much of this, reportedly told MLQ that "the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero," according to Startup Fortune. Secondary reports of his page say some reproducibility items, such as comparing proof exports across separate sandboxed builds, were still listed as open. Anthropic has not issued a formal statement, and Alpöge has not said which Claude model or how much compute was used.

sections.h: What has and has not been checked
table: Accepted by Lean kernel, con-leche, con-ron, others
Not covered by the joint statement
None; AI-written draft runs past 250,000 pages, not posted
Requires publication, two years, general acceptance
sections.note: From the Lean community joint statement; tool and axiom details from secondary reports (Datastudios, Unite.AI) of Sutherland's MIT verification page. Draft length per Alpöge's note as reported by Startup Fortune.

p: **Kernel:** the small core of a proof assistant that actually checks each logical step. Everything else (tactics, automation, AI) can be wrong without harm, as long as the kernel accepts the final result.
**Inert export:** the finished proof written out as plain data and checked separately, so the checker never runs the project's own code. It rules out a proof that games the checker.
**Axioms:** the starting assumptions. The three listed are the standard ones nearly all of Mathlib uses; an extra one would have been a red flag.

This is as strong a correctness guarantee as formal methods offer today, and it comes from the people who maintain the tools, not from Anthropic. On the narrow question "is this a valid proof of the Riemann hypothesis as Mathlib states it," the evidence now points firmly to yes.

What it does not give is understanding. Mathematicians value a proof for the ideas it reveals, and nobody can yet explain this one; Terence Tao said on Nov 20 that digesting it will take time. Michael Rubinstein of Waterloo has reportedly started a 164-page explainer of the zeta-function part, but that rests on one key inequality taken from the Lean code. Expect the next stage to be people extracting a human argument from the machine one. Separately, Alessandro Masullo's human-written GRH draft remains unverified and under major revision.
Alpöge's promised write-up and talks (no dates), Sutherland's remaining reproducibility checks, any Anthropic statement on the model used, and whether anyone formally checks the generalized version.

stories.headline: UN weapons talks end with an agreement to 'elaborate' rules on AI-run autonomous weapons by 2028, but no commitment to a binding treaty
stories.summary: The 128-member Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons missed UN chief Guterres's 2026 target for starting negotiations after the US, Russia, and Israel resisted.
stats: New deadline to elaborate an instrument
Nations that wanted binding rules now

p: A weeklong UN meeting in Geneva under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) ended Saturday, Nov 21, after talks ran through the night. States agreed to the "elaboration" of a possible instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028, per AFP and AP. Some countries rejected the word "negotiate," and the text does not commit anyone to binding rules. Secretary-General António Guterres, who leaves office at the end of 2026, had set 2026 as the deadline to launch negotiations.

Nearly 100 nations wanted swift adoption of legally binding rules, AFP reports, and seven (Brazil, Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, Panama) proposed opening negotiations, per AP. Key arms producers including the United States, Russia, and Israel opposed the push; Russia's procedural objections led to some formal sessions being called off. Because the CCW works by consensus, any one state can block a decision.

Reactions split. UN disarmament chief Izumi Nakamitsu called it a "significant achievement" and urged work to start "as early as Monday." Swiss chair Julien Thoeni said it showed "multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results." Stop Killer Robots called the mandate "watered down," and Beatrice Fihn of Lex International called it "pushing the can down the road for two more years."
**Lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS):** weapons that can select and attack targets without a human approving each strike, for example drones that identify targets by themselves.
**Elaborate vs. negotiate:** in diplomatic text, "negotiate" signals drafting a treaty to sign; "elaborate" is vaguer and leaves the form, including whether it is binding, open.
**Consensus:** every state must accept a decision, so the most reluctant country sets the ceiling.

Formal talks on this have run since 2014, and this is another two-year extension rather than a treaty. The countries most able to build these weapons are the ones keeping the language soft, and they prefer national guidelines. The real constraints on military AI in the near term will come from national policies, procurement rules, and bilateral understandings, like the human-involvement principle Treasury Secretary Bessent said Trump and Xi agreed to, which has not been published in writing.

For AI companies selling to defense, this means no international rulebook to design to before 2028 at the earliest, and continued pressure through their own usage policies and government contracts instead.

Whether the work Nakamitsu urged actually starts this week, how the 2028 text treats human control, and whether frustrated states take the issue to the UN General Assembly, where consensus is not required.

stories.headline: Amazon nears a $7.5 billion deal for Decart, a startup that makes AI run efficiently across chips, the FT reports
stories.summary: A deal could be announced as early as this week, per the Financial Times; it would help Amazon make its own Trainium chips a stronger alternative to Nvidia.
stats: Decart's valuation in May, per Mint

p: The Financial Times reported Saturday, citing people familiar, that Amazon is in advanced talks to acquire Decart, a San Francisco-based AI startup founded in 2023, in a deal worth about $7.5 billion that could be announced as early as this week. Seeking Alpha's summary of the FT report says the deal is still at risk of collapse. Talks at about $7 billion were first reported in October.

Decart, led by co-founder and CEO Dean Leitersdorf, builds software that runs AI models more efficiently and makes it easier to move workloads between different chips, plus real-time video models (Lucy, Oasis). It already runs its live video models on Amazon's Trainium chips. Israeli outlet Calcalist reported Nov 18 that the package would mix cash, shares, and deferred payments, some tied to performance targets, with arrangements to keep founders at Amazon for five years. Amazon has not confirmed.
**Trainium:** Amazon's in-house AI chip, offered on AWS as a cheaper alternative to Nvidia GPUs.
**Deferred and performance-based payments (earnouts):** part of the price is paid later only if targets are hit or people stay. The headline number is usually the maximum, not cash on day one.

The hard part of switching off Nvidia is not the chip but the software: most AI code is tuned for Nvidia's CUDA. Buying a team whose specialty is moving models between chips is a direct attack on that lock-in, and the timing lands as Nvidia's stock and leadership are under heavy pressure. Decart's own claims that Trainium beats leading GPUs on its workloads are customer testimonials published by AWS, not independent benchmarks.
At nearly double its May valuation for a three-year-old company, the price also shows big tech is still paying up for AI talent even as public AI stocks fall.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, a roughly $33 billion network security company, Reuters and Bloomberg report
stories.summary: Reported late Friday; Zscaler jumped about 17% after hours and CrowdStrike fell, with no terms disclosed and no deal guaranteed.

p: On Friday, Nov 20, after the market close, Bloomberg and then Reuters (citing two people familiar) reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler. Reuters said "No deal is guaranteed, and the discussions could still end without an agreement"; Bloomberg's sources said it could come together soon. No price or cash-versus-stock structure has been reported, and neither company commented.

Zscaler rose about 17% in after-hours trading and CrowdStrike fell about 8%, per Reuters. CrowdStrike's largest acquisition so far was SGNL, at $970 million, per SiliconANGLE, so this would be many times bigger than anything it has done. The two companies already have a product partnership.
**Endpoint security:** protecting individual devices (laptops, servers), CrowdStrike's core business with its Falcon platform.
**Zero trust network access (ZTNA):** checking every connection to a company's apps instead of trusting anyone inside the network, Zscaler's core business and a VPN replacement.

Reuters frames it as filling CrowdStrike's biggest gap, network security, to compete with Palo Alto Networks as customers cut the number of security vendors. The AI angle is real but mostly a pitch for now: the argument is that AI-driven attacks need one platform seeing both devices and network traffic, and that AI security agents work better with more combined data. Nothing is agreed, and a deal this large would face a long antitrust review.

stories.headline: A second Riemann claim appears: a 940-page, AI-free draft from a Stanford mathematician, and readers using AI flag problems within hours
stories.summary: AMS president Ravi Vakil posted Alessandro Masullo's unfinished proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis the same day Levent Alpöge's Claude-assisted Lean proof surfaced; neither has been verified.
stats: Alpöge theorems checked at MIT so far

p: On Nov 20, Stanford's Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a blog entry titled "Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH" with a 940-page draft called "The Music of the Primes". It claims a proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which includes the ordinary Riemann hypothesis as a special case. Scientific American describes Masullo as a young mathematician at Stanford; XenoSpectrum, reading the draft's acknowledgments, says he began the work in his first year of graduate school there under Brian Conrad. Vakil describes the proof as human, with no AI involved.

Conrad has been giving Masullo feedback for months, Scientific American reports, and confirmed the blog's details to the magazine. He was careful: "To judge the success of the method requires the paper to reach a stage of more final revision," he said, adding that "it's undergoing major revision." The draft itself is visibly unfinished: per XenoSpectrum, sections 13.1 and 13.2 are headings only and a footnote on page 522 notes that the statement of a key theorem and the proofs of the main theorems still need to be added. Vakil wrote that he makes no claim the strategy is correct and asked others to inspect it. About eight hours later he updated the post to say several people had reported problems, found "with help from different AI models," according to LavX News.

The same day, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's Claude-assisted claim (covered Friday) kept moving through checks. XenoSpectrum, citing MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland's verification page, reports that two independent Lean kernels (nanoda and con-leche) accepted the full exported proof, that con-leche confirmed the five main theorem statements match their targets, and that only Lean's three standard axioms are used. The Comparator run and a strict-mode recheck were still in progress. Scientific American's piece says other mathematicians are expressing skepticism and that neither proof has been verified.

table: Lean archive of 175,187 files; compiles; standard axioms only
Comparator run, strict kernel recheck, human-readable paper
Five theorems, including ordinary RH and Dirichlet L-functions
940-page draft, unfinished; major revision under way
Months of feedback from Brian Conrad; problems reported after release
sections.note: From Scientific American (via Yahoo), XenoSpectrum's reading of Sutherland's report and the Masullo draft, and LavX's account of Vakil's update. XenoSpectrum notes the draft's target (all Hecke L-functions) is broader than the Dirichlet-level statements checked at MIT.

p: **Generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH):** the claim that a whole family of functions related to the zeta function, called L-functions, all have their nontrivial zeros on the same critical line. Proving GRH would prove the ordinary Riemann hypothesis too.
**Independent kernel:** a separate program that rechecks a Lean proof from scratch. If several kernels written by different people accept it, a bug in any one checker becomes an unlikely explanation.
**Statement check:** confirming that the theorem the computer proved is really the famous statement, not a subtly different one. This is what Comparator automates and why experts are still waiting.

Two very different routes to the same problem arrived on the same day, and they are failing or passing different tests. Masullo's draft has a respected reviewer but is incomplete by its own text, and the early problem reports are a normal part of reading a 940-page manuscript, not yet a verdict. Alpöge's proof is the reverse: machines have now checked it more thoroughly than most human proofs ever get, but no human can yet read it, and the full statement match is still pending.

A detail worth noticing: AI models helped readers find problems in the human proof within hours. Whatever happens to either claim, AI is becoming part of how mathematics is checked, not only how it is produced. Nobody is owed a Clay prize yet; its rules require publication and a waiting period with broad acceptance.
The Comparator report on Alpöge's archive, Vakil's further updates on the reported gaps in Masullo's draft, and whether either author posts a revised, readable paper.

stories.headline: Alpöge and NYU's Tristan Buckmaster say AI helped them show Navier-Stokes can blow up with no outside force, but the proof's certificate is not out
stories.summary: The claim, reported by Scientific American, targets the loophole critics saw in OpenAI's September result, which needed a specially chosen force stirring the fluid.

p: NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge posted on Mastodon on Nov 20 at 8:37 a.m. EST that they have an AI-assisted proof that the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids like water and air move, can blow up (develop an infinite value in finite time) without any external force, according to LavX News, citing a Scientific American article by Peter Hall. Buckmaster said the write-up is unpolished because they "couldn't risk waiting." The certificate backing the result had not been released; LavX says it would follow. Which AI system did the work, and whether the proof is checked in Lean, was not stated in what we could read.

This is the next round of a fight from September. On Sept 8, OpenAI said an internal model had produced a 166-page, Lean-checked proof of finite-time blowup for Navier-Stokes. Buckmaster said OpenAI had told him that result was for forced Navier-Stokes, with a smooth force added, and that an OpenAI researcher pushed to drop Alpöge as a co-author on their own related work because he works at Anthropic, per his public statement and TechCrunch. OpenAI denied seeing their work before it was released, while saying it could not rule out that de-identified product usage data helped its models. Many experts considered the forcing an unrealistic loophole in the prize wording.

**Blowup:** a solution that starts smooth and then, in finite time, has some quantity (like velocity) shoot to infinity. Showing it can happen answers one version of the Clay Millennium Navier-Stokes problem.

**Forced vs unforced:** a forced problem lets you add an outside push, chosen by the mathematician, into the equations. That extra freedom makes blowup easier to engineer. The unforced version, with nothing stirring the fluid, is the one most mathematicians consider the real question.
**Certificate:** the data or formal proof file that lets others check a computer-assisted result independently.

Treat this as a claim, not a result. There is no certificate, no paper we could find, and no named outside expert has checked it. What it shows is how fast frontier math is now moving, and how much of it involves AI and one researcher, Alpöge, who is attached to both this and the Riemann claim in the same week. If it holds up, unforced blowup would be a far bigger deal than the forced result, because it removes the objection that the answer depended on a hand-picked force.
It also keeps the priority dispute alive. Labs now race on famous open problems with huge compute budgets, and credit, data use, and authorship rules have not caught up.
Release of the certificate and a full write-up, which AI tools they used, and responses from fluid-dynamics experts and from OpenAI.

stories.headline: Bessent says Trump and Xi agreed humans must be involved in major military decisions made with AI
stories.summary: The Treasury secretary described the understanding on CNBC after the Shenzhen meeting; no written text or Chinese confirmation has been reported.

p: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday, Nov 20, that President Trump and Xi Jinping agreed at their Shenzhen meeting that "humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes" and that "the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," Reuters reported. SI is the administration's term for super intelligence. He also said "no major military operation should be launched without a human being involved," and that competition for AI supremacy would not affect the agreement.

On chips, Bessent said Nvidia's H200 remains the most advanced chip China can buy with a license, noted "a paucity of orders from the Chinese on the H200s," and said "the remote access has been curtailed," referring to Commerce's Nov 16 move to restrict Chinese firms renting AI compute in overseas data centers. He said the spying allegations involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang did not come up. Reuters says a fourth Trump-Xi meeting is expected in mid-December at the G20 in Miami.

This is the first concrete AI result reported from a summit that ended without a joint statement, and it is thin. It rests on one official's verbal account, with no document, no definition of "major," no mention of nuclear command and control, and no reported Chinese confirmation. Biden and Xi reached a similar understanding in 2024 limited to nuclear weapons decisions; this one sounds broader but vaguer.

Still, a stated shared line on human control is a useful hook. It gives both sides something to build on in the stalled incident-reporting channel and at the G20, and something to point to if either side's military AI use is questioned.

Whether Beijing confirms the understanding, whether it appears in writing before or at the G20 in Miami, and whether it ties into the White House's pending legal definition of super intelligence, due Nov 28.

stories.headline: The SEC's Nvidia investigation is examining its accounting, Reuters reports, and the stock falls 14% in its worst day since January 2025
stories.summary: Two people briefed on the matter told Reuters the agency's enforcement staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues; neither the SEC nor Nvidia commented.

p: Reuters reported Friday afternoon that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of Nvidia is looking at the company's accounting, citing two people briefed on the matter. SEC enforcement staff are "scrutinizing potential accounting issues," Reuters wrote, but it could not determine which issues, or when the inquiry opened. The Wall Street Journal had reported on Tuesday that the SEC was probing Nvidia, without being able to say what the focus was. Yahoo Finance relays a WSJ report that the probe includes whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. The SEC declined to comment; Nvidia did not respond.

Nvidia was already down more than 6% before the story ran and closed at $125.53, down 14.01%, its seventh straight loss and its worst day since the DeepSeek selloff of January 2025, per Yahoo Finance. Yahoo puts Friday's loss of market value at about $485 billion and the week's at nearly $900 billion, a record one-week loss (the prior record was $573 billion, per Dow Jones Market Data). Nvidia is now the fourth most valuable US company, behind Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet. Shares rose about 3.6% after hours.

This lands on a company already without its founder as CEO. Reuters describes Jensen Huang as ousted; interim CEO Colette Kress, the former CFO, said on Tuesday's earnings call that Nvidia would be "far more selective" about financing deals with AI companies. Yahoo notes Nvidia delayed its quarterly 10-Q filing to "the coming weeks" and that its earnings release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

table: Hugging Face deal under DOJ review
sections.note: Price, value, rank, and receivables figures from Yahoo Finance; Hugging Face figure and probe details from Reuters.

p: **SEC enforcement inquiry:** an investigation by the agency's enforcement division into possible securities-law violations. It can end with no action, a settlement, or charges. Reuters notes that investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without enforcement.

**10-Q:** the quarterly report a public company files with the SEC, with full financial statements and risk disclosures. Filing it late, while a board committee investigates, usually means the company wants its auditors and lawyers to finish reviewing something first.

**Days sales outstanding:** how long, on average, customers take to pay. A rising number can mean customers are getting more generous payment terms, which matters when a supplier is also financing its customers.

The key unknown is what the SEC is looking at, and nobody has reported it. Reuters and Yahoo both list the obvious candidates without tying them to the probe: Nvidia's 2025 switch to reporting revenue by customer headquarters rather than billing address (which removed Singapore, per the FT about half of sales by billing location), and its "circular" deals, where Nvidia invests in or guarantees financing for customers who then buy its chips. Yahoo says plainly it is not clear which, if any, the SEC is focused on.

The market reaction is about uncertainty stacking up: a CEO exit tied to a scandal, a delayed filing, an internal board probe, DOJ antitrust and export reviews, Treasury's demand for answers, upcoming congressional testimony, and now accounting. Any one of these might come to nothing. Together they make Nvidia's numbers harder to trust until the 10-Q lands, and Nvidia's revenue is the single best gauge of AI infrastructure spending. For people building with AI, nothing changes this week: chips already ordered keep shipping. The risk is slower financing for the smaller cloud and data center companies Nvidia has been backing.

The 10-Q filing and whether it restates anything; the board committee's findings; Treasury Secretary Bessent's 10-day window for answers, which ends around Nov 25; and the Huang and Teter congressional interviews on Dec 1 and 2.

stories.headline: An MIT mathematician recompiles the claimed Riemann proof and finds only Lean's standard axioms, but the key statement check is still pending
stories.summary: Andrew Sutherland says the chance anything is fishy is "approximately zero"; Kevin Buzzard is still waiting for a Comparator run, and no human-readable paper exists.

p: Since Friday morning's edition, the first outside check of Levent Alpöge's claimed Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis has come in. Andrew Sutherland of MIT recompiled the full archive of 175,187 Lean files without errors, and the Lean kernel accepted the result using only Lean's three standard axioms (propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound), according to Scientific American as quoted by AI Weekly and The Bay Area Brief, and Brazilian outlet Antihype. Sutherland told Scientific American: "Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero."

The check experts most want is not done. Imperial College's Kevin Buzzard said he is still waiting for a Comparator run, which confirms the code does not quietly redefine symbols in the theorem statement and that it checks on more than one Lean kernel. Terence Tao of UCLA said verification "will take some time," per the BBC as cited by The Bay Area Brief, and called the proof enormous and apparently reliant on the full force of the Langlands program, per Antihype. Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal called Alpöge's four-page write-up "garbled," and Oxford's James Maynard said that if the work "fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics," both per Nature as cited by The Bay Area Brief.

Two new details on how it was done: Alpöge used a non-public version of Claude over about six weeks, per reports, and no model name has been given. He also wrote that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the timing, a day after the company's stock debut, calling it "horrible" and saying "there is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false." Anthropic did not immediately comment to Nature.

table: Full proof compiles, standard axioms only
Done by Sutherland; Comparator not yet
Named expert endorsement of the math
sections.note: Compiled from AI Weekly, The Bay Area Brief, Antihype, and Kingy, which relay Scientific American, Nature, and the BBC. We could not read the Scientific American and Nature articles directly.

p: **Lean kernel:** the small core of the Lean proof assistant that does the final step-by-step check of every proof. It is deliberately simple so it can be trusted; if the kernel accepts a proof, the logic holds given the axioms used.

**The three standard axioms:** propext (two statements that imply each other are equal), Classical.choice (you can pick an element from any nonempty collection), and Quot.sound (a rule about quotient types). Almost all of Mathlib uses them; an extra axiom would be a red flag.

**Langlands program:** a vast web of conjectures and theorems linking number theory and symmetry. Saying a proof uses its full force means it leans on some of the deepest machinery in modern math, which makes human checking much harder.

This moved the claim forward meaningfully. A clean recompile with only standard axioms rules out the most common way a formal proof cheats. What remains is whether the formal statement being proved is really the Riemann hypothesis and whether nothing in the 175,000 files tampers with the definitions it relies on. That is exactly what Comparator checks, and it is why Buzzard is not yet convinced. Sutherland's confidence is notable because he is an outside expert, but it is one person's view of one build.

Even if Comparator passes, mathematicians will want to understand the proof, and right now there is no readable paper, only a short note its own author calls partly paraphrased from Claude. A verified-but-unexplained proof would still be historic, and it would also raise a new problem for math: how to learn from a result no one fully understands. Until the Comparator report is public, treat this as very promising, not settled.

The Comparator report, the Lean community's Zulip discussion, Tao's further comments, any Anthropic statement, and whether Alpöge posts a full write-up.

stories.headline: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26-billion-parameter open model that runs on a 32GB Mac by reusing its middle layers three times
stories.summary: The Apache 2.0 model activates 3.4 billion parameters per token and posts strong agentic coding scores on the lab's own tables, with candid warnings about its reliability.

p: Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on Nov 20, the smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small from earlier this month. Weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0, with a separate acceptable-use policy. It takes text and images and outputs text, with a context window of up to 1 million tokens, per the model card. It is also available through the lab's Tinker platform, where Kingy reports prices of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output.

The design is unusual. It is a 24-layer mixture-of-experts transformer (each token goes to 8 of 128 experts per layer), but the middle 12 layers run three times in a row with the same weights. So each token passes through 48 layer applications while the file only stores 24 layers. The lab says this lifts effective active parameters from 3.4 billion to about 5.4 billion per token. The checkpoint is a single file of about 20GB in mixed 4-bit and 8-bit formats; the lab lists Apple silicon Macs with 32GB or more, a DGX Spark, or GPUs with 32GB of memory as supported.

sections.note: All from Thinking Machines' model card, including competitor scores as the lab reports them. Kingy reports Vals ranks it 38th of 43 on the Vals Index.

p: **Looped (weight-shared) layers:** running the same block of layers several times per token, so the model thinks "deeper" without storing more weights. It saves memory and download size, not compute: the hardware still does all 48 passes.

**Active parameters:** in a mixture-of-experts model, only some experts run for each token. Active parameters are the ones actually used per token, which sets speed and cost; total parameters set the memory needed to hold the model.
**NVFP4 and MXFP8:** compact 4-bit and 8-bit number formats for storing weights. Smaller formats let a big model fit on a laptop, with some loss of precision.

The headline is that a model that scores near the best open models of its size on coding agents now fits on a mid-range Mac. Two cautions. First, the benchmarks are the lab's own, and the independent picture is more modest: on the Artificial Analysis index it ties Qwen3.8-27B, and Vals ranks it near the bottom of its leaderboard. Second, the lab's own limitations section is unusually blunt: it says the model is more likely than larger ones to state wrong facts with confidence, can get stuck in reasoning loops, and "may take destructive actions, such as deleting or overwriting files, without confirmation." Run it in a sandbox.

The looped design is the part to remember. Reusing layers trades storage for compute, and the lab notes that it lets the model do more computation without visible reasoning tokens, which is a mild concern for anyone relying on reading a model's chain of thought. The 32GB figure covers loading the model, not using its full 1 million token context, which needs much more memory.
Independent speed tests of looped models in Ollama and llama.cpp, which the lab says are new and vary by hardware, and whether other labs adopt layer looping.

stories.headline: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis, with a Lean proof that outside checks have not yet confirmed
stories.summary: Levent Alpöge posted a four-page note and a 175,000-file Lean archive; no independent mathematician has vouched for it yet, and a full machine check was still running Friday.
stats: Lean files in the archive (Kingy count)
Oct 6 to Nov 16, per the note
Clay prize, after 2 years of acceptance

p: Levent Alpöge, a number theorist on Anthropic's staff, posted a short note on his website on Thursday night saying: "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis." The note also claims the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, a family of related functions. Alongside it he posted a 14-part archive of Lean code he says formalizes the full proof, per Quantum Zeitgeist, Interesting Engineering, and Kingy, which downloaded the archive.

According to the note as reported, the work ran 41 days, from Oct 6 to Nov 16, and the working material grew past 250,000 pages. Alpöge says he directed the project toward its approach and that Claude later made advances beyond his own command of some of the mathematics; he says Claude suggested a key parameter choice. He also writes that parts of his sketch are paraphrased from Claude's summaries and that he has not yet mastered all the surrounding mathematics. None of the reports name which Claude model was used, and none quote an official Anthropic statement.

Checking started immediately. An independent GitHub project confirmed the downloaded files match the archive and that the main theorem statements compile against Mathlib, Lean's shared math library. But as of Friday morning, a run of Comparator, a tool that replays the proof and lists every axiom it relies on, was still in progress, per Kingy. The green check that finished at 15:07 UTC covered only independently written versions of the theorem statements, not Alpöge's proof itself.

sections.note: Archive figures from Kingy's download; timeline from Alpöge's note as quoted by Quantum Zeitgeist and Superpower Daily; Clay rules and status from Interesting Engineering and Kingy.

p: **Riemann hypothesis:** a 167-year-old conjecture that all the 'nontrivial' zeros of the Riemann zeta function sit on one vertical line. It controls how evenly prime numbers are spread out, and thousands of published results assume it. It is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems.

**Lean and Mathlib:** Lean is a proof assistant, software that checks each step of a proof written as code. Mathlib is its community library of definitions, including an official definition of the Riemann hypothesis. A proof that compiles with no gaps or extra axioms is logically valid for the statement it proves.

**Axiom check:** a proof can quietly assume something unproven by adding it as an axiom. Tools like Comparator list every axiom a proof uses, so reviewers can confirm only Lean's standard ones remain.

This is a claim, not a result. Extraordinary math claims have a long history of falling apart, and the Riemann hypothesis has drawn many failed proofs. What is different here is that the claim arrives with a machine-checkable proof, so the core question can be settled by software within days, not by referees over years. Two things have to hold: the full archive must compile with no hidden axioms or gaps, and the formal statement must really be the Riemann hypothesis. The second check is easier than it sounds because the archive targets Mathlib's existing definition, which Alpöge did not write.

Even if the Lean check passes, mathematicians will want a human-readable argument, and Alpöge says the proof is extremely long and will need simplifying. A machine-verified proof tells you the result is true, not why. Formal recognition (the Clay prize) requires peer-reviewed publication and two years of acceptance.

If it holds, it would be the strongest evidence yet that AI systems can do frontier research, not just assist. That is also why skepticism is warranted: the claimant works at the company whose model gets the credit, and the account of how much Claude did versus Alpöge is his alone so far. Treat any headline saying 'AI solved the Riemann hypothesis' as premature until the axiom report is public and independent number theorists weigh in.
Disclosure: Latent is produced with Claude, which is made by Anthropic.

The Comparator axiom report on the full archive; whether named number theorists (Alpöge thanks Manjul Bhargava and Peter Sarnak, who have not publicly commented) review it; any Anthropic statement; and an arXiv paper.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO closes at $93.5 billion after banks buy all their extra shares, as the stock falls about 12% toward its $83 offer price
stories.summary: The raise reaches about $119.5 billion with the $26 billion private placement to seven chip and cloud companies, which also closed Friday.

p: Anthropic said Friday it closed its IPO of 1.127 billion Class A shares at $83, including the underwriters' full option to buy 147 million more. Gross proceeds were about $93.5 billion, of which about $91.6 billion goes to Anthropic; the rest went to existing shareholders who sold 23.6 million shares. The $81.3 billion figure reported at pricing covered the base deal only.

It also closed the concurrent private placement: 313.3 million non-voting Class N shares at $83, about $26 billion, bought by AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC Partners. Those shares are not registered for public trading.

The stock did not hold Thursday's gains. Reuters reported ANT fell to $85 by 12:20 p.m. ET, about 12.5% below Thursday's $97.17 close and about 2% above the offer price. Reuters cited data showing retail investors traded more than $750 million of the stock on Thursday; Anthropic has said less than 20% of shares went to retail buyers.

sections.note: Offering figures from Anthropic's closing announcement. Stock prices from Reuters. Commitment figures from Anthropic's S-1/A filings as analyzed by The Inference and AI Infra Credit.

p: **Greenshoe (over-allotment option):** banks sell up to 15% more shares than the base deal, then either buy them from the company (if the stock trades well) or buy them back in the market to support the price (if it falls). Exercising the full option this quickly means the banks chose to take new shares from Anthropic.

**Private placement:** shares sold directly to chosen investors outside the public offering. Here the buyers are mostly Anthropic's own suppliers, which is part of why critics talk about 'circular' AI deals.

Anthropic now has a war chest of about $91.6 billion from the IPO plus the placement, the largest any company has raised in one listing. It needs it: its filings show about $900.9 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, and about $186 billion of that sits behind termination rights or unmet conditions. One example is a $34.9 billion Lambda contract that either side can now cancel after Lambda missed a lease deadline, though Anthropic says it does not intend to.

The day-two drop says more about the market than the company (see the next story). Still, anyone who bought at Thursday's open near $111 was down more than 20% by Friday midday. A stock that trades near its offer price in its first week can draw in the banks' stabilization efforts; here, with the greenshoe already exercised, that buffer is smaller.
Disclosure: Latent is produced with Claude, which is made by Anthropic. This is not investment advice.

stories.headline: S&P 500 and Dow briefly enter a correction and the Nasdaq erases its 2026 gains, as Nvidia slips below Alphabet in value
stories.summary: Chip stocks led a seventh straight losing day for the S&P 500; Nvidia fell about 7% and AMD and Micron around 9% to 12% by midday.
stats: Nvidia, now No. 4 in the US

p: The selloff in AI stocks that followed Anthropic's debut deepened Friday. At about 1 p.m. ET, the S&P 500 was down more than 2% and the Nasdaq Composite 3.4%, while the Dow fell about 0.6%, Yahoo Finance reported. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow briefly crossed into correction territory, 10% below their peaks, and the Nasdaq gave back all of its gains for the year. The S&P was headed for a seventh straight loss, its longest streak since 2020, per Bloomberg as cited by Startup Fortune.

Chips were hit hardest. Around midday, Nvidia was down about 7% (Startup Fortune put it at $135.34, down 7.3%), AMD about 9% to 11%, Micron 10% to 12%, and Broadcom about 6%, per Coinpedia and Startup Fortune. Earlier, Reuters reported Nvidia had fallen behind Alphabet to become the fourth most valuable US company, at about $3.4 trillion against Alphabet's $3.44 trillion, and was on course for its longest losing streak since 2008 and a seventh straight weekly decline.

Reasons cited vary. Reuters said Nvidia's first earnings report since co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation failed to ease worries about its leadership and how durable AI spending will be, and that investors are moving toward companies with established cloud and software revenue. Yahoo also pointed to inflation, a possible US government shutdown in December, Middle East conflict, last week's major tech outages, and doubts about AI profitability. The Cboe volatility index (VIX) rose above 31, its highest since March.

sections.note: Intraday figures, not closes. Index moves from Yahoo Finance at about 1 p.m. ET; chip moves from Coinpedia (about noon ET) and Startup Fortune, which differ slightly; Nvidia and Alphabet values from Reuters at 10:30 a.m. ET; streak and weekly figures from Bloomberg via Startup Fortune.

p: **Correction:** a fall of 10% or more from a recent peak. A bear market is 20% or more. They are conventions, not economic signals by themselves.
**VIX:** an index of how much volatility options traders expect in the S&P 500 over the next month. Readings above 30 usually mean real fear; the long-run average is near 20.

The AI trade is unwinding in the order you would expect: the companies most directly tied to AI spending (chips, memory, neoclouds) are falling hardest, while the Dow, with less tech weight, holds up better. Alphabet passing Nvidia fits the Reuters read that investors now prefer companies that earn money from AI through existing businesses over those selling the picks and shovels.

For people building with AI, nothing about the technology changed this week. The risk to watch is financing: much of the data center buildout is funded by debt and by deals where suppliers invest in their customers, and those get harder when stock prices and confidence fall. Remember these are intraday numbers; the close may differ meaningfully.
This is not investment advice.
Friday's close and whether the S&P ends the week in a correction; Monday's open; and any change in AI companies' borrowing plans, including Nscale's planned December listing.
